questions.stem: A developer is building an archiving service that must encrypt PDF files of 2 MB to 50 MB before they are written to an on-premises object store. The developer calls the {{t:AWS KMS}} {{code:Encrypt}} API with a file's contents as the plaintext, but the request is rejected because the plaintext exceeds the 4,096-byte limit. Every file must still be protected by the team's symmetric {{t:customer managed key}}. Which approach will encrypt the files in the MOST efficient way?

choices.text: Split each file into 4 KB chunks, call {{code:Encrypt}} on every chunk, and concatenate the resulting ciphertexts.
choices.explanation: This technically works, but a 50 MB file would need about 12,800 KMS calls, each a network round trip that counts against the account's request quota and is billed. {{code:Encrypt}} is intended for small items such as data keys, not bulk data.

choices.text: Call {{code:GenerateDataKey}}, encrypt the file locally with the plaintext data key, discard that plaintext key, and store the returned encrypted data key next to the ciphertext.
choices.explanation: This is envelope encryption: one KMS call per file regardless of size. The data key is encrypted under the KMS key, so the KMS key never leaves KMS and the file never crosses the network to KMS. Later, {{code:Decrypt}} on the stored encrypted data key recovers the key needed to read the file.

choices.text: Switch to an asymmetric RSA KMS key so that larger payloads can be passed to {{code:Encrypt}}.
choices.explanation: Asymmetric keys make the problem worse: an RSA_4096 key with OAEP SHA-256 padding accepts at most 446 bytes of plaintext, and asymmetric operations have much lower request quotas than symmetric ones.

choices.text: Call {{code:GenerateRandom}} to obtain 256 random bits, encrypt the file locally with them, and store the key in plaintext beside the ciphertext so that no further KMS calls are needed.
choices.explanation: Storing the plaintext key beside the ciphertext defeats the encryption entirely. {{code:GenerateRandom}} returns bytes that are not protected by any KMS key, so the file is no longer tied to the customer managed key and there is nothing to call {{code:Decrypt}} on.

questions.explanation: KMS {{code:Encrypt}} accepts at most 4 KB of plaintext because symmetric KMS keys never leave KMS and the API exists to protect small secrets such as data keys. Anything larger uses envelope encryption: {{code:GenerateDataKey}} returns a plaintext data key plus a copy encrypted under the KMS key; you encrypt locally, keep only the encrypted copy with the ciphertext, and call {{code:Decrypt}} on that copy when you need to read the data. Use {{code:GenerateDataKeyWithoutPlaintext}} when the component that creates the key will not encrypt right away, and let the {{t:AWS Encryption SDK}} implement the whole pattern for you instead of hand-rolling it.

references.title: AWS KMS concepts – envelope encryption
AWS KMS API Reference – Encrypt
AWS KMS API Reference – GenerateDataKey

questions.stem: A company runs a data-processing {{t:AWS Lambda}} function in account B. The function must read objects from an {{t:Amazon S3}} bucket in account A. The objects are encrypted with {{t:SSE-KMS}} using a {{t:customer managed key}} that also belongs to account A. The bucket policy already allows the function's execution role to call {{code:s3:GetObject}}, yet every read fails with an {{code:AccessDenied}} error that originates from {{t:AWS KMS}}. Which combination of changes will allow the function to read the objects? (Choose TWO.)

choices.text: Add a statement to the key policy in account A that allows the function's execution role in account B to call {{code:kms:Decrypt}}.
choices.explanation: The key policy is the primary access control for a KMS key. Until the key owner's policy names the external account or principal, no policy in account B can grant any access to the key. S3 calls {{code:kms:Decrypt}} on the caller's behalf when it serves an SSE-KMS object, so the role needs that permission.

choices.text: Create an alias for the key in account B so that the function can reference the key with a short name.
choices.explanation: Aliases are scoped to the account and Region that own the key; you cannot create an alias for a key in another account, and a cross-account caller must identify the key by its key ARN or alias ARN, never by a bare alias name. Here S3 selects the key, so the function never references it at all. Aliases grant no permissions.

choices.text: Have the function call {{code:CreateGrant}} on the key at startup to give its own role {{code:kms:Decrypt}} permission.
choices.explanation: A principal can only create a grant if it is already allowed {{code:kms:CreateGrant}} by the key policy, which the role in account B is not. Grants are meant for temporary, programmatic delegation by a principal that already has access, not as a way to acquire access.

choices.text: Attach an identity-based IAM policy to the function's execution role in account B that allows {{code:kms:Decrypt}} on the key's ARN.
choices.explanation: Cross-account KMS access is two-sided: after the key policy admits account B, the caller's own identity-based policy in account B must also allow the action on the key ARN. Without it the role has no permission even though the key policy would accept it.

choices.text: Add a {{code:kms:ViaService}} condition to the key policy so that only requests that arrive through Lambda in account B are allowed.
choices.explanation: {{code:kms:ViaService}} restricts which AWS service may use the key on a principal's behalf; it never grants the missing permission. Worse, the request here is made through S3, not Lambda, so a Lambda-only condition would block exactly the calls that need to succeed.

questions.explanation: Using a KMS key across accounts requires BOTH the key policy in the owning account to allow the external account or principal AND an identity-based policy in the calling account to allow the principal to use the key; an IAM policy in another account can never grant access to a key on its own, because the key policy is what admits that account (the default key policy delegates to IAM only within the key's own account). Reference a key in another account by its key ARN or alias ARN, never by a bare alias name. Grants are for temporary delegation by someone who already has {{code:kms:CreateGrant}}, and {{code:kms:ViaService}} only narrows access to calls that come through a named service such as S3 or Lambda.

references.title: Allowing users in other accounts to use a KMS key
Key policies in AWS KMS
Grants in AWS KMS

questions.stem: A developer's application encrypts records client-side with data keys generated from a symmetric {{t:customer managed key}} in {{t:AWS KMS}}. A new compliance rule requires the key material to be rotated at least once a year. The developer worries that millions of existing records will become unreadable after rotation and is planning a yearly batch job that re-encrypts every record. Which approach satisfies the compliance rule with the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.text: Enable automatic key rotation on the customer managed key and leave the existing records as they are.
choices.explanation: Automatic rotation creates new key material on a schedule (yearly by default) but KMS retains every previous version and uses the right one to decrypt existing ciphertext. The key ID and ARN do not change, nothing needs to be re-encrypted, and no code or job is required.

choices.text: Create a new customer managed key every year, repoint the application's key alias to it, and run the batch job to re-encrypt all records under the new key.
choices.explanation: Manual rotation through an alias is a valid pattern, but the re-encryption job is unnecessary: ciphertext encrypted under the old key still decrypts as long as that key exists. Managing a growing set of keys plus a yearly data migration is far more overhead than a single rotation setting.

choices.text: Switch the application to the {{t:AWS managed key}} for the service, because AWS managed keys are rotated automatically every year.
choices.explanation: AWS managed keys ({{code:aws/service}} aliases) do rotate yearly, but they can only be used by the AWS service that created them; your own code cannot call {{code:GenerateDataKey}} or {{code:Encrypt}} with one, and you cannot edit their key policy.

choices.text: Import the company's own key material into a new KMS key each year and update the application to use the new key ID.
choices.explanation: Keys with imported key material are not eligible for automatic rotation, so this makes rotation a manual yearly process in which you also have to track material expiry and key IDs. It adds operational risk rather than removing it.

questions.explanation: Automatic rotation of a customer managed key generates new key material (every 365 days by default; the period is configurable, and on-demand rotation is also available) while retaining all earlier material, so old ciphertext decrypts transparently and new data is encrypted with the latest material. Rotation never re-encrypts existing data and never changes the key ID or ARN; manual rotation, by contrast, means a brand-new key with a new ARN, which is why applications should reference keys through aliases. AWS managed keys rotate yearly too but are usable only by their owning service, and AWS owned keys are not visible in your account at all.

references.title: Rotating AWS KMS keys
AWS KMS concepts – customer managed, AWS managed and AWS owned keys

questions.stem: An {{t:AWS Lambda}} function consumes messages from an {{t:Amazon SQS}} queue and encrypts each message body with a fresh data key from a symmetric {{t:customer managed key}} before forwarding it to a downstream system. During a traffic spike the function processes about 30,000 messages per second and begins failing with {{code:ThrottlingException}} from {{t:AWS KMS}}, because the shared per-Region quota for symmetric cryptographic requests is lower than that. The function already retries with exponential backoff. Which change will eliminate the throttling in the MOST cost-effective way?

choices.text: Open a case in {{t:Service Quotas}} to raise the account's symmetric cryptographic request quota in the Region to at least 30,000 requests per second, and keep the existing retry logic.
choices.explanation: A quota increase is a legitimate fallback, but it keeps one billed KMS request per message, so the KMS bill scales linearly with traffic, and very large increases are not guaranteed. It is the more expensive of the two workable options.

choices.text: Create one customer managed key per Lambda execution environment so that the requests are spread across more keys.
choices.explanation: The symmetric request quota is shared across all KMS keys in the account and Region, so adding keys adds no capacity; it only adds monthly key charges and key-management burden.

choices.text: Switch the function to an asymmetric RSA key, which is not counted against the shared symmetric quota.
choices.explanation: Asymmetric operations have their own, far lower shared quota (about 1,000 requests per second for RSA keys) and higher per-request pricing, so the function would be throttled sooner and each message would take longer to encrypt.

choices.text: Use the {{t:AWS Encryption SDK}} with data key caching so that one data key is reused for a bounded number of messages before a new {{code:GenerateDataKey}} call is made.
choices.explanation: Data key caching reuses a data key across many messages within limits you set (maximum age, number of messages, bytes), cutting KMS requests by orders of magnitude. Fewer requests means both no throttling and a smaller KMS bill, with the security trade-off bounded by the cache limits.

questions.explanation: KMS returns {{code:ThrottlingException}} when calls exceed the shared per-account, per-Region quota for symmetric cryptographic operations (10,000 requests per second by default, 20,000 in several large Regions and 100,000 in us-east-1, us-west-2 and eu-west-1; older study material still quotes 5,500, 10,000 and 50,000). Exponential backoff absorbs short bursts, but sustained volume is solved by making fewer calls: data key caching in the {{t:AWS Encryption SDK}} reuses a data key across operations, and for S3 the equivalent is {{t:S3 Bucket Keys}}. Ask for a quota increase only when every operation genuinely needs a fresh KMS call.

references.title: AWS KMS request quotas
AWS Encryption SDK – data key caching

questions.stem: A healthcare company stores patient reports in an {{t:Amazon S3}} bucket. Auditors require that every object be encrypted with the company's {{t:customer managed key}} in {{t:AWS KMS}} so that each use of the key is recorded, and that no client can read or write the bucket over an unencrypted connection. Any upload that does not satisfy these requirements must be rejected rather than fixed afterwards. Which combination of actions will enforce the requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Choose TWO.)

choices.text: Set the bucket's default encryption to {{t:SSE-S3}} so that every new object is encrypted automatically.
choices.explanation: {{t:SSE-S3}} is already the default for every new object, but it uses keys that S3 manages: there is no key policy to control and no per-request KMS entry in the audit trail. Default encryption also never rejects an upload; it only fills in a method when the request specifies none.

choices.text: Add a bucket policy statement that denies {{code:s3:PutObject}} unless the {{code:s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption}} condition key equals {{code:aws:kms}} and the {{code:s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption-aws-kms-key-id}} condition key equals the company's key ARN.
choices.explanation: These condition keys mirror the {{code:x-amz-server-side-encryption}} and {{code:x-amz-server-side-encryption-aws-kms-key-id}} request headers. An explicit Deny in the bucket policy rejects any upload that is not {{t:SSE-KMS}} with the required key, with no code to maintain.

choices.text: Enable an {{t:S3 Bucket Key}} on the bucket so that objects are encrypted with the company's key at a lower cost.
choices.explanation: An {{t:S3 Bucket Key}} reduces the number of KMS requests (and therefore cost) that {{t:SSE-KMS}} generates by using a bucket-level data key for a limited time. It is a cost optimisation and enforces neither the encryption method nor TLS.

choices.text: Require clients to use {{t:SSE-C}} so that each request carries the company's key in its headers.
choices.explanation: With {{t:SSE-C}} the client supplies a raw key on every request over HTTPS and S3 does not store it. The key is not a KMS key, so there is no key policy and no KMS audit record, and every client would have to be given the key material: more work and less control.

choices.text: Add a bucket policy statement that denies all {{code:s3:*}} actions when the {{code:aws:SecureTransport}} condition key is {{code:false}}.
choices.explanation: {{code:aws:SecureTransport}} is false for requests made over plain HTTP. A Deny keyed on it forces every read and write to use TLS, which is exactly the encryption-in-transit requirement, again with no custom code.

choices.text: Deploy a scheduled {{t:AWS Lambda}} function that lists the bucket daily, deletes objects that are not encrypted with the company's key, and emails the owners.
choices.explanation: This is a detective control that acts up to a day after the fact, violates the requirement to reject non-compliant uploads, does nothing about TLS, and adds code to maintain.

questions.explanation: Enforcement in S3 lives in the bucket policy: a Deny on {{code:s3:PutObject}} keyed on the {{code:s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption}} and key-ID condition keys rejects any upload that is not {{t:SSE-KMS}} with the required key, and a Deny keyed on {{code:aws:SecureTransport}} being false rejects plain HTTP. Know the trade-offs: {{t:SSE-S3}} is the free default with no key control or per-call audit; {{t:SSE-KMS}} adds key policies, CloudTrail entries and KMS request charges that {{t:S3 Bucket Keys}} reduce; {{t:SSE-C}} shifts all key handling to the client; client-side encryption keeps plaintext out of S3 entirely but puts the crypto code in your application.

references.title: Using server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys (SSE-KMS)
Bucket policy examples – requiring encryption in transit
Reducing the cost of SSE-KMS with Amazon S3 Bucket Keys
Using server-side encryption with customer-provided keys (SSE-C)

questions.stem: A developer must expose a REST API on {{t:Amazon API Gateway}} through the custom domain api.example.com over HTTPS. The security team requires a certificate issued by a publicly trusted certificate authority, and nobody on the team wants to track certificate expiry dates by hand. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.text: Purchase a certificate from a third-party certificate authority, import it into {{t:AWS Certificate Manager}}, and associate it with the API Gateway custom domain name.
choices.explanation: Imported certificates work with API Gateway, but ACM never renews a certificate it did not issue. The team would have to buy, validate and re-import a new certificate before every expiry, which is exactly the manual tracking they want to avoid.

choices.text: Generate a self-signed certificate with OpenSSL, import it into {{t:AWS Certificate Manager}}, and associate it with the custom domain name.
choices.explanation: A self-signed certificate is not issued by a publicly trusted CA, so browsers and SDK clients reject it. It also has no managed renewal.

choices.text: Request a public certificate for api.example.com in {{t:AWS Certificate Manager}} using DNS validation, and associate it with the API Gateway custom domain name.
choices.explanation: ACM public certificates are free for use with integrated services such as API Gateway, and as long as the DNS validation CNAME stays in place ACM renews them automatically and deploys the renewed certificate to the custom domain. Nothing to track.

choices.text: Request an exportable public certificate in ACM, export the private key, and install the certificate on an {{t:Amazon EC2}} proxy that terminates TLS in front of the API.
choices.explanation: Exportable ACM certificates are charged per domain name, add an EC2 tier to run and patch, and although ACM renews them, each renewed certificate must be exported and redeployed by the team or by automation the team builds. They exist for workloads that cannot use ACM-integrated services, which is not the case here.

questions.explanation: {{t:AWS Certificate Manager}} issues publicly trusted certificates at no charge for ACM-integrated services (API Gateway custom domains, {{t:Elastic Load Balancing}}, {{t:Amazon CloudFront}}) and renews them automatically when DNS validation is in place; imported certificates are never renewed by ACM. A standard ACM public certificate cannot be exported to run on EC2 or on premises; for that you request a paid exportable certificate, use {{t:AWS Private CA}}, or bring your own. Also remember that a certificate for a CloudFront distribution or an edge-optimized API Gateway domain must be requested in us-east-1, while a Regional API domain needs a certificate in the API's Region.

references.title: What is AWS Certificate Manager?
Setting up custom domain names for REST APIs
AWS Certificate Manager introduces exportable public certificates

questions.stem: A developer stores the credentials that several {{t:AWS Lambda}} functions use to connect to an {{t:Amazon RDS}} for PostgreSQL database. A new security policy requires the password to be changed automatically every 30 days without downtime, and the functions must always be able to retrieve the current value. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST development effort?

choices.text: Store the password as a {{code:SecureString}} parameter in {{t:AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store}} and attach a parameter policy that expires it every 30 days.
choices.explanation: Parameter policies (advanced tier only) can send an {{t:Amazon EventBridge}} notification when a parameter is about to expire, but {{t:Parameter Store}} has no built-in rotation: nothing changes the database password or writes a new value. You would still have to write that code.

choices.text: Store the credentials in {{t:AWS Secrets Manager}}, turn on rotation using the AWS-provided rotation function for Amazon RDS, and set the rotation schedule to 30 days.
choices.explanation: Secrets Manager supplies ready-made rotation Lambda functions for RDS engines (and managed rotation for RDS master user passwords). It changes the database password, stores the new version under {{code:AWSCURRENT}} and keeps the old one as {{code:AWSPREVIOUS}}, so callers that fetch the secret always get a working value without any rotation code.

choices.text: Store the password as a {{code:SecureString}} parameter in {{t:Parameter Store}} and create an {{t:Amazon EventBridge}} schedule that invokes a custom Lambda function to change the password in RDS and update the parameter.
choices.explanation: This works and is the usual way to rotate a Parameter Store value, but the rotation logic (new password, ALTER USER, update parameter, handle failures) is custom code that the team must write, test and maintain. Secrets Manager already provides it.

choices.text: Store the password in each function's environment variables, encrypt them with a {{t:customer managed key}}, and redeploy the functions with a new password every 30 days.
choices.explanation: Encrypting environment variables protects them at rest, but {{code:GetFunctionConfiguration}} still returns the value to anyone allowed to read the function and use the key, nothing is automatic, and every rotation becomes a coordinated redeploy of all functions.

questions.explanation: {{t:AWS Secrets Manager}} is the service with rotation built in: it ships rotation function templates for RDS, Redshift and DocumentDB, supports managed rotation for RDS master user passwords, and uses staging labels ({{code:AWSCURRENT}}, {{code:AWSPENDING}}, {{code:AWSPREVIOUS}}) so clients keep working during a rotation. {{t:Parameter Store}} {{code:SecureString}} parameters are KMS-encrypted, free in the standard tier and support hierarchical names such as /app/prod/db retrieved with {{code:GetParametersByPath}}, which makes them ideal for configuration and low-churn secrets, but rotation needs your own EventBridge-plus-Lambda code. Secrets Manager charges per secret per month and per 10,000 API calls.

references.title: Rotate AWS Secrets Manager secrets
AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store

questions.stem: A high-traffic {{t:AWS Lambda}} function calls {{code:GetSecretValue}} on every invocation to fetch a database credential from {{t:AWS Secrets Manager}}. The function runs millions of times a day, and both the Secrets Manager API charges and the extra latency per invocation have become significant. The credential is rotated automatically every 7 days, and the function must begin using a rotated value within a few minutes of the rotation without being redeployed. Which solution meets these requirements with the FEWEST code changes?

choices.text: Add the {{t:AWS Parameters and Secrets Lambda Extension}} layer to the function, fetch the secret over HTTP from the extension's local endpoint, and set {{code:SECRETS_MANAGER_TTL}} to a few minutes.
choices.explanation: The extension caches secrets in memory inside the execution environment and refreshes them when the TTL expires, so most invocations make no Secrets Manager call and a rotated value is picked up within the TTL. The only code change is swapping the SDK call for a local HTTP request.

choices.text: Read the secret once in the initialization code outside the handler and keep it in a module-level variable for the lifetime of the execution environment.
choices.explanation: This removes the per-invocation call, but an execution environment can live for hours, so the function would keep using a stale credential long after rotation and start failing. Adding a timed refresh to fix that means writing and testing your own cache logic, which is more code than the extension.

choices.text: Copy the secret into a {{t:Lambda}} environment variable encrypted with a {{t:customer managed key}} and read it from {{code:process.env}} in the handler.
choices.explanation: Environment variables are fixed at deploy time, so a rotated credential is never picked up without a redeploy, which the requirements rule out. They are also visible to anyone with {{code:GetFunctionConfiguration}} access unless the console's encryption helpers are used, and even then the value is static.

choices.text: Move the credential to a {{code:SecureString}} parameter in the {{t:AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store}} standard tier and call {{code:GetParameter}} on every invocation instead.
choices.explanation: Standard-tier {{code:GetParameter}} calls at standard throughput are free, so the bill would drop, but there is still one network call per invocation, so latency is unchanged, and {{t:Parameter Store}} cannot perform the automatic rotation the credential relies on.

questions.explanation: The {{t:AWS Parameters and Secrets Lambda Extension}} is a layer that exposes a local HTTP endpoint (port 2773 by default) and caches Secrets Manager and Parameter Store values with configurable TTLs ({{code:SECRETS_MANAGER_TTL}}, {{code:SSM_PARAMETER_STORE_TTL}}, 300 seconds by default); requests must carry the {{code:X-Aws-Parameters-Secrets-Token}} header set to {{code:AWS_SESSION_TOKEN}}. It gives you caching with bounded staleness and no cache code. A module-level variable is the hand-rolled alternative for values that never change. Secrets never belong in plaintext environment variables or in the repository: anyone who can read the function configuration or the source can read them.

references.title: Use AWS Secrets Manager secrets in AWS Lambda functions
Using Parameter Store parameters in AWS Lambda functions
Securing Lambda environment variables

questions.stem: A developer deploys an application with an {{t:AWS SAM}} template that creates an {{t:Amazon RDS}} instance and an {{t:AWS Lambda}} function. The database password must be supplied to the instance's {{code:MasterUserPassword}} property at deployment time, but it must not appear in the template in source control, in the deployment command, or in the stack's parameter values shown in the {{t:AWS CloudFormation}} console. Which approach is the MOST secure?

choices.text: Declare a template parameter for the password with {{code:NoEcho}} set to true and pass the value with {{code:--parameter-overrides}} at deploy time.
choices.explanation: {{code:NoEcho}} masks the value in the console and in {{code:DescribeStacks}}, but the plaintext still has to be typed into or stored by the deployment command, so it ends up in shell history, CI configuration or build logs.

choices.text: Store the password in {{t:AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store}} and declare a template parameter of type {{code:AWS::SSM::Parameter::Value<String>}} that points at it.
choices.explanation: SSM parameter types are resolved at deploy time and the resolved value is displayed with the stack's parameters in the console, and they do not support {{code:SecureString}} parameters, so the password would have to be stored unencrypted.

choices.text: Store the password in {{t:AWS Secrets Manager}} and set {{code:MasterUserPassword}} to a CloudFormation dynamic reference to that secret.
choices.explanation: A dynamic reference of the form {{code:resolve:secretsmanager:secret-id:SecretString:password}} (wrapped in CloudFormation's double-brace syntax) is substituted at stack-operation time. The template, the CLI command and the stack parameters contain only the reference, never the password.

choices.text: Place the password in the template's {{code:Mappings}} section and restrict read access to the repository to the deployment team.
choices.explanation: This is a plaintext secret in source control, visible in every clone, pull request and template preview; restricting repository access reduces but does not remove the exposure, and it fails the requirement outright.

questions.explanation: CloudFormation dynamic references pull a value from {{t:AWS Secrets Manager}} ({{code:resolve:secretsmanager:secret-id:SecretString:json-key}}) or from a {{t:Parameter Store}} {{code:SecureString}} ({{code:resolve:ssm-secure:parameter-name:version}}) while the stack operation runs, so the secret is never written into the template, the command line or the stack parameters. {{code:ssm-secure}} references are supported only for the resource properties listed in the dynamic-references documentation ({{code:MasterUserPassword}} among them), whereas {{code:secretsmanager}} references work in any resource property. {{code:NoEcho}} only masks a value that already had to be supplied in plaintext. For RDS in particular, setting {{code:ManageMasterUserPassword}} to true lets RDS generate and store the password in Secrets Manager for you.

references.title: Using dynamic references to specify template values
CloudFormation template Parameters syntax

questions.stem: A multi-tenant SaaS application uses envelope encryption with a single symmetric {{t:customer managed key}} in {{t:AWS KMS}}. After a suspected incident, the security team asks the developer two questions: which IAM principal called {{code:Decrypt}} on the key during a two-hour window last week, and, for each of those calls, which tenant's data was being decrypted. Which combination of actions will allow the developer to answer both questions? (Choose TWO.)

choices.text: Enable {{t:Amazon CloudWatch Logs}} for the KMS key and filter the log group for {{code:Decrypt}} events.
choices.explanation: KMS has no per-key logging to CloudWatch Logs. KMS API activity is recorded by {{t:AWS CloudTrail}}; you can forward a trail to CloudWatch Logs for searching, but CloudTrail is the source and must be used either way.

choices.text: Prepend the tenant identifier to the plaintext before encrypting it so that the identifier is encrypted together with the data.
choices.explanation: With envelope encryption the plaintext never reaches KMS; KMS only sees the encrypted data key. Anything embedded in the plaintext is invisible to KMS and therefore absent from the audit record.

choices.text: Search {{t:AWS CloudTrail}} event history, or the trail's logs in S3, for {{code:Decrypt}} events on the key's ARN during the window and read the {{code:userIdentity}} element of each event.
choices.explanation: Every KMS API call is a CloudTrail management event that records the caller's identity, the key ARN, the time and the request parameters. The {{code:userIdentity}} element answers the 'who' question directly.

choices.text: Enable {{t:AWS Config}} recording for the KMS key and review the key's configuration timeline for the window.
choices.explanation: AWS Config records configuration changes to the key (key policy, rotation setting, state), not cryptographic API calls, so it cannot show who decrypted what.

choices.text: Pass an encryption context such as {{code:tenant-id}} on every {{code:GenerateDataKey}} and {{code:Decrypt}} call, because the encryption context is written to the CloudTrail event for each call.
choices.explanation: Encryption context is non-secret key-value metadata that KMS cryptographically binds to the ciphertext as additional authenticated data and logs in plaintext in CloudTrail. Each {{code:Decrypt}} event then shows which tenant's data key was being decrypted.

questions.explanation: Who used a KMS key is always a {{t:AWS CloudTrail}} question: every {{code:Decrypt}}, {{code:Encrypt}} and {{code:GenerateDataKey}} call is logged with the caller's identity, the key ARN and the encryption context. Encryption context is a set of non-secret key-value pairs that acts as additional authenticated data: the same context must be supplied to decrypt, which also prevents a data key encrypted for one tenant from being decrypted under another tenant's context. Because the context is logged in plaintext, never put secrets in it.

references.title: Logging AWS KMS API calls with AWS CloudTrail
AWS KMS concepts – encryption context
